sysd-msg-020.title: Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command
sysd-msg-020.text:
A car goes from for sale to sold. That is an event: a data point, a significant change in state. It announces the change and says nothing about what should happen next.

Event-driven architecture builds whole systems from announcements like this. Producers publish events to a router, the router filters them and pushes them to consumers, and the consumers use them to reflect the change in the system. Usually the events travel through a {{ref:sysd-msg-051}}, which publishes and delivers them asynchronously. The publisher is unaware of who consumes an event, and the consumers are unaware of each other.

That ignorance is the point. It keeps services loosely coupled, decouples producers from consumers and makes it easy to add a new consumer. Systems built on events are highly scalable and distributed, horizontal scaling gets simpler, and the whole is more resilient to failure. Typical uses are metadata and metrics, server and security logs, integrating heterogeneous systems, and fanout and parallel processing. Widely used technologies include {{ref:sysd-msg-036}}, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS and Google PubSub.

The price is real. Guaranteed delivery, error handling and exactly-once, in-order processing are all hard. Such systems are complex in general and inherently hard to test.

sysd-msg-127.title: Domain-driven design: code that speaks the business's language
sysd-msg-127.text:
A loan system might have loan applications, customers and a method called accept offer. That is domain-driven design in miniature. The structure and language of the code, down to class and method names, match the business domain, modeled with input from the domain's experts. Experts, users and developers share one ubiquitous language, used both in the model and in describing requirements.

The approach rejects a single unified model. It divides a large system into separate areas, each with its own model, an idea developed in {{ref:sysd-msg-085}}. An aggregate binds objects under a root entity: outside objects may reference only the root, which checks that changes stay consistent. Combined with {{ref:sysd-msg-024}} and {{ref:sysd-msg-021}}, aggregate roots take a command as input and output one or more events.

Before any of that, event storming helps. In this workshop, stakeholders, domain experts and developers map the domain's events to discover subdomains, boundaries and aggregates. Critics say the approach demands much isolation and encapsulation, and Microsoft recommends it only for complex domains where the model clearly helps.

sysd-msg-022.title: Event store: a database of nothing but events
sysd-msg-022.text:
In an event store, the events are the only real facts. Everything else is derived from them. An entity's state at any point in its history is rebuilt by replaying its events in order. Objects that aggregate the recorded data are not stored. Runtime code builds them on the fly by traversing the history, then discards them.

Stored events never change, even erroneous ones. The only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values. Backdated events, which take effect before earlier ones, are easier to handle this way. Only the new event is stored, and the code redetermines the objects from the new facts, with no rollback. The disadvantage is that code may need to re-instantiate every object in memory each time a service call arrives for a given dossier or policy.

One newspaper website keeps every article, image and byline in an event store. It denormalizes the raw data into views fed to ElasticSearch nodes for website searches. {{ref:sysd-msg-036}} is also a distributed event store and stream-processing platform.

sysd-msg-021.title: Event sourcing: keep the history, derive the present
sysd-msg-021.text:
Storing only the current state forgets how things got there. Event sourcing keeps the whole series of actions instead. It changes the programming paradigm from persisting states to persisting events, recorded in an append-only {{ref:sysd-msg-022}}. That store acts as the system of record and can be used to materialize the domain objects.

Do not confuse it with {{ref:sysd-msg-020}}, as people constantly do. Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data. Event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries. Event sourcing is one of several patterns for implementing an event-driven architecture.

Keeping the full history pays off. It gives audit trails that can enable compensating actions, lets data be reconstituted from the event store after a failure, and suits real-time reporting and high-compliance audit logs. The costs are an extremely efficient network infrastructure and a reliable way to control message formats, such as a schema registry, because different events carry different payloads.

In a microservice system, a service such as the shopping cart emits events to a Kafka broker acting as the event store. Other services consume them, each determining its own domain model. A stream can also be fed by {{ref:sysd-msg-041}}. There, a connector pulls data from tables and transforms it into events, which are pushed to Kafka for other sinks to consume.

sysd-msg-128.title: The fallacies of distributed computing
sysd-msg-128.text:
Programmers new to distributed applications invariably make the same false assumptions. L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems listed them as the fallacies of distributed computing. The original list begins with four: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure. It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.

Each false belief has a price. Assume the network is reliable, and applications get little error handling. They stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns. Ignore latency and the packet loss it causes, and developers allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth. Ignore bandwidth limits, and bottlenecks appear.

Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy. Richards and Ford added three more: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work, and {{ref:sysd-reliab-098}} is optional.

sysd-msg-026.title: Broker or mediator: two ways to wire an event system
sysd-msg-026.text:
Who is in charge when events flow? Event-driven architecture has two primary topologies, broker and mediator, and the two can be combined in a hybrid model.

In the broker topology there is no orchestrator. Components broadcast events to the entire system, and the reward is higher performance and scalability. In the mediator topology a central orchestrator controls the workflow of events, and the reward is better control and error handling.

Put plainly, the choice trades the speed and scale of the first against the control and error handling of the second.

sysd-msg-030.title: When consumers fail and events vanish
sysd-msg-030.text:
A consumer chokes on an event. What now? One answer is a separate error-handler processor. The failing consumer sends the erroneous event to it asynchronously and moves on. The processor tries to fix the event and sends it back to the original channel. If it fails, it sends the event to an administrator for inspection. The catch is that events resubmitted this way are processed out of sequence.

Data loss is the other danger. A component crashes before it has processed an event and handed it to the next component, so the event is dropped and never reaches its destination. To minimize this, persist events while they are in transit and dequeue them only after the next component acknowledges receipt. These features are known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.

Event-driven systems are also susceptible to {{ref:sysd-msg-128}}, misconceptions that can cause significant problems in development and deployment.

sysd-msg-029.title: Simple, stream and complex event processing
sysd-msg-029.text:
A mature event-driven architecture often uses all three general styles of event processing together: simple, stream and complex.

In simple event processing, a notable event tied to a specific, measurable change of condition initiates downstream actions. It drives the real-time flow of work and reduces lag time and cost. In event stream processing, ordinary events such as orders or RFID transmissions are screened for notability and streamed to subscribers. This drives the real-time flow of information and in-time decisions.

Complex event processing looks at patterns of simple and ordinary events to infer that a complex event has occurred, and then takes action. The events may cross event types and span a long period, and their correlation may be causal, temporal or spatial. It needs sophisticated event interpreters, pattern definition and matching, and correlation techniques. It is commonly used to detect business anomalies, threats and opportunities.

A fourth approach, online event processing, uses asynchronous distributed event logs to process complex events and manage persistent data. It reliably composes related events across heterogeneous systems and allows very flexible distribution patterns with high scalability and strong consistency. What it cannot do is guarantee upper bounds on processing time.

sysd-msg-028.title: Inside an event: header, payload and how much to carry
sysd-msg-028.text:
An event is made of a header and a body, also called the payload. The header may hold the event name, a time stamp and the event type. The payload provides the details of the detected state change, and it should not be confused with the logic applied in reaction to the event.

The design question is how much to put in the payload. Put in all the necessary attributes, and speed and scalability improve. The risks are data consistency problems from multiple systems of record, stamp coupling and bandwidth issues at scale. Put in only keys or IDs, and consumers fetch the data from sources such as databases. That minimizes bandwidth and coupling, but it is less scalable and slower because of the queries.

These two methods are ends of a spectrum, not a binary choice. Architects must size payloads to the needs of the event consumers.

sysd-msg-129.title: Command–query separation: asking should not change the answer
sysd-msg-129.text:
Asking a question should not change the answer. Bertrand Meyer built command–query separation on that idea. Every method should be either a command that performs an action or a query that returns data, but not both. A method returns a value only if it has no side effects.

Queries never change state, so any query can be called anywhere, such as in assertions, without fear of side effects. It has limits. A combined method such as a stack's pop can be more convenient. In multithreaded code, separate increment and value calls leave a race condition that a locked increment-and-return avoids. The pattern in {{ref:sysd-msg-024}} generalizes the principle to services.

sysd-msg-024.title: CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads
sysd-msg-024.text:
A command is an instruction to perform a task that changes the system, and it returns only success or failure. A query requests information without changing state or causing side effects. Command Query Responsibility Segregation, or CQRS, extends {{ref:sysd-msg-129}} to the level of services, with separate interfaces for sending commands and queries. The two play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.

Many systems push the split into the data. Read models process queries and write models process commands, usually tailored to their tasks and often held in physically separate stores. CQRS is often combined with event sourcing. Then the store of events is the write model and the official source of information, and the read model offers materialized, highly denormalized views.

The benefits are independent scaling of read and write workloads, easier optimization, clear boundaries and no complex joins when querying. The drawbacks are a more complex design, possible message failures or duplicate messages, the challenge of {{ref:sysd-scale-097}}, and more maintenance effort.

sysd-msg-027.title: Domain events and integration events
sysd-msg-027.text: Some events stay home, and some travel. Domain events signify important occurrences within one business domain. They are restricted to one area with its own model (see {{ref:sysd-msg-085}}), and they are vital for preserving business logic. Their payloads are typically lighter, with only the information needed for processing. Integration events communicate changes across different such areas and are crucial for keeping data consistent across the entire system. Their payloads tend to be more complex, with additional attributes, because the needs of their potential listeners differ significantly.

sysd-msg-033.title: The four layers an event passes through
sysd-msg-033.text:
An event passes through four logical layers: the producer, the channel, the processing engine and downstream activity. The producer senses a fact and represents it as an event message. Converting data from sources as diverse as email clients and sensors into one standard form is a significant task.

The channel carries events from the producer to the engine. Several channels can be open at once and are read asynchronously, with events queued for later processing. The engine selects and executes the reaction, such as ordering a product and notifying personnel when stock is low. The downstream layer shows the consequences, such as an email.

sysd-msg-031.title: Event granularity: how many events, how much detail
sysd-msg-031.text:
How many events should a system publish, and how much should each say? Finding the right number is difficult. Too many detailed events can overwhelm the system and make the event flow hard to analyze, a problem worse when rollbacks are required. Overly consolidated events make consumers do unnecessary processing and send unnecessary responses.

Mark Richards recommends considering the impact of each event and whether consumers need to read the payload to decide their actions. In a compliance check, publishing only compliant and non-compliant events can suffice. Each event is then processed only by relevant consumers, and unnecessary workload falls.

sysd-msg-034.title: Getting a synchronous answer from an event-driven system
sysd-msg-034.text: Sometimes the caller needs an answer now, even in a system built on events. Synchronous transactions in an event-driven architecture can be built on the request-response paradigm, implemented in two ways. One uses two separate queues, one for requests and one for replies, and the event producer must wait until it receives the response. The other uses one dedicated ephemeral queue, a short-lived one, for each request.

sysd-msg-035.title: The timeout antipattern: too short, too long
sysd-msg-035.text:
How long should a caller wait? Both answers hurt. A short timeout may fail legitimate requests prematurely and lead to complex workarounds. A long timeout gives slow error responses and a poor user experience. This difficulty of setting timeout values in distributed systems is the timeout antipattern.

The pattern in {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}} can address it. It watches service health through heartbeats, synthetic transactions or real-time usage, which enables faster failure detection.

sysd-msg-023.title: Fixing events by adding events: the double timeline
sysd-msg-023.text: In an event store you cannot edit history, so how do you fix a mistake? Give each event two dates: the valid date, when it became valid, and the transaction date, when it was entered into the database. A correcting event carries the new values, keeps the event date of the event it corrects, and has a different transaction date. This ensures reproducibility at every moment in time, even in the period before the correction took place. It also allows situations that were based on erroneous events to be reproduced, if required.

sysd-msg-130.title: Apache Avro: compact binary data that carries its schema
sysd-msg-130.text: Avro is a row-oriented framework, developed within Apache's Hadoop project, for two jobs: turning data into bytes, covered in {{ref:sysd-msg-125}}, and making remote calls, covered in {{ref:sysd-msg-018}}. Hadoop uses it both as a format for persistent data and as a wire format between its nodes and from client programs to its services. Schemas are defined in JSON and data is serialized in a compact binary format. Data can be stored with its schema, so a serialized item can be read without knowing the schema ahead of time. Unlike Thrift and {{ref:sysd-msg-006}}, Avro needs no code-generation step when a schema changes, and its binary encoding is smaller and faster.

sysd-msg-032.title: Event schema evolution: changing events without breaking consumers
sysd-msg-032.text:
Event-driven systems look loosely coupled in space, time and synchronization, yet they stay tightly coupled, through subscriptions and patterns, to the semantics of the event schema and values. That is why changing events is hard. Schemas can become inconsistent across services, and compatibility must hold while the system is updated gradually.

Strategies include versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility. Adapters can translate events between old and new formats, so processing stays consistent across components. One format that needs no code-generation step when a schema changes is {{ref:sysd-msg-130}}.

sysd-msg-025.title: McDonald's event platform: a registry, a gateway, regional clusters
sysd-msg-025.text:
McDonald's platform is a tour of this chapter's problems, with an answer to each.

The first problem is keeping events consistent. An event registry defines a standardized schema, and custom SDKs (software development kits) process events and handle errors. That ties together the shape of an event ({{ref:sysd-msg-028}}), the way that shape changes over time ({{ref:sysd-msg-032}}) and the failures a consumer can hit ({{ref:sysd-msg-030}}).

The second is control. An event gateway verifies who is calling and what each caller may do. Utilities and tools fix events, keep the cluster healthy and perform administrative tasks.

The third is scale. A regional architecture on AWS provides global availability. Within a region, producers shard events by domain, the sharding idea behind {{ref:sysd-scale-087}}, and each domain is processed by its own MSK cluster. Each cluster auto-scales on MSK metrics such as CPU usage, using a workflow built on step-functions and re-assignment tasks.

The thing to remember: the platform splits events by domain, with a cluster for each. A registry and its SDKs keep every producer speaking one standard schema.

openers.event-driven-architecture-event-sourcing: Instead of one part of a system calling another and waiting for an answer, parts can announce that something happened and let others react. That is event-driven architecture: components communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously. This chapter follows the idea outward. It covers storing the full series of actions as the source of truth, and splitting commands that change state from queries that only read it. It also looks at how to wire such a system with or without one orchestrator, what an event carries, and how consumers and events fail.

reviews.event-driven-architecture-event-sourcing: The chapter's pieces fit around one habit: announce what happened and let others react. An event has a header and a payload, passes through producer, channel, processing engine and downstream activity, and is processed in simple, stream or complex ways. Event sourcing keeps those events as the source of truth, and CQRS splits commands from queries, often with read models built from the events. A broker topology gives performance and scalability, a mediator gives control, and either must cope with failing consumers, lost events, timeouts and changing schemas. McDonald's platform shows many of these pieces at work together: a registry for schemas, SDKs for errors, a gateway, and clusters split by domain.
